title: Nanofabrication throughput for mechanical metamaterials
bottleneck: Nanoarchitected mechanical metamaterials achieve extraordinary strength-to-weight ratios, but fabrication relies on two-photon lithography and electron-beam writing that produce only cubic millimeters per hour at costs exceeding $10,000 per cubic centimeter. Scaling to structural components needs square meters of material, a throughput gap of roughly six orders of magnitude. Faster methods like projection micro-stereolithography gain speed but lose the true 3D lattice architectures that give metamaterials their properties.
why_it_blocks: Ultralight, ultra-strong lattices could transform aerospace, vehicles, and protective equipment, cutting fuel use and material consumption. The throughput wall confines them to laboratory samples and tiny high-value parts, so none of those system-level benefits materialize.
current_state: Roll-to-roll nanoimprint and self-assembly via block copolymers show promise for larger areas, though mostly limited to 2.5D extrusions rather than true 3D lattices. Capital costs above $10 million per production line keep the technology out of reach for most manufacturers.
